Hence, the question raised here is how external shocks on life circumstances impact on remembered utility or subjective wellbeing? And what is the role of group membership in adjusting to these external shocks? In effect, given that the external shocks brought about by climate change are affecting the process of resource allocation and consumption on a global scale, the response needs to be at a pace and scale that can match its global outreach. Group bias can accelerate or decelerate the pace and scale of climate policy inter­ ventions and hence global decision-making from the bottom-up. First, let’s look at how external shocks impact on Subjective Well-Being (SWB), used as a proxy for remembered utility here. Taking the 2008 financial crisis as an example of an external shock on life circumstances, the behavioural nature of this event is linked to simultaneous housing and financial bubbles related to group behaviour at the bottom and top of the income distribution, respectively. Such event impacted on the SWB threshold of various social groups. The presence of a thresh­ old in relation to SWB came to light with the Easterlin Paradox (Easterlin, 1974, 1995, 2005). In Easterlin’s (1995: 35) own words: “within a country at a given time those with higher incomes are, on average, happier. However, raising the incomes of all does not increase the happiness of all”, and beyond a certain income level, any further increase in income makes little or no difference to overall SWB levels (Easterlin, 1995; Pouwels et  al., 2008). It is however not clear how individuals adjust back to that threshold when economic shocks occur. The role of relative income has been the most common way to explain the Easterlin Paradox (McBride, 2001). Individuals compare personal income to their peers, so that the impact of the increase in their own absolute income on SWB can be cancelled out by their peers’ relative income increases. Hence, such explanation signals a group effect on how individuals assess and re-assess their life circumstances in comparison with “peers”. In other words, group membership means that individuals share comparable cir­ cumstances and experiences with group members that can thus be qualified as peers. Peer comparison leads individuals to compare themselves with other individuals with whom they perceive to belong to the same group(s). Such group effect is 2 This section draws from Charles et al. The literature on group membership shows that group behaviour tends to be more self-centred and predictable than individual behaviour (Bornstein et al., 2004; Charness & Sutter, 2012; Brown & Yang, 2015). In the experimental laboratory set­ ting, Bornstein et  al. (2004) provide evidence from experiments with strategic games that group members are more rational in terms of maximising the payoff for each group member, and that they are less pro-social toward other groups. Group players assume that players in other groups behave similarly which triggers a self-­ reinforcing norm to maximise the group’s aspirations for higher payoffs. Outside the laboratory setting, Brown and Yang (2015) show that the relative social value between men and women leads women to be underestimated by the betting system in jump racing, where, as jockeys they can compete equally. In the social setting, group membership strongly affects the individual’s perception of life circumstances through peer comparison. As pointed out by Dolan et al. (2008: 105), “perceptions of our circumstances can be very important predictors of life satisfaction”. In effect, in their comprehensive literature review of the factors associated with SWB, the word “perception” itself appears six times for six different factors. This is important when considering the impact of a peer or group effect on individual behaviour because individual choice is based on remembered utility rather than experienced utility. At the level of remembered utility, group membership influences individual SWB by affecting the hierarchy of life domains in the SWB function. For example, the dominant norm for self-employed individuals may be to value their job on a higher scale than employed individuals. Here, the argument is not concerned with the heterogeneity versus homogeneity of groups but rather that, since remembered utility is affected by peer comparison, individual perception of life circumstances is influenced by the hierar­ chy of the life domains of the groups to which they belong. Then, since each indi­ vidual belongs to multiple groups, the ranking of the life domains should be revealed at the group rather than individual level, and it should also differ according the intersection of groups investigated, for example, a female self-employed plumber versus a male employed plumber. In effect, as pointed out by Crenshaw (1989), the intersectionality of group memberships can lead to different normative outcomes compared with considering groups separately. Together with peer comparison, adaptation to life circumstances through adap­ tive preferences or hedonic adaptation has been highlighted as another important factor that will return SWB to its individual threshold (Clark et al., 2005; Clark, 2006; Binder & Coad, 2010, 2011). From the happiness perspective, the “endow­ ment effect” (Huck et al., 2005) or “treadmill effect” Kahneman and Tversky (2000) shows that people have a tendency to get used to life circumstances in the sense that they adapt their perceptions and judgments to get back to their individual threshold. Further evidence of adaptive preferences has been gathered by Burchardt (2005) in the context of constant and increasing incomes, linking the argument to the risk-­ aversion of individuals. The argument put forward by Rabin (2001) however is that risk aversion is intrinsically linked to utility derived from wealth rather than income. In effect, March (1988) shows that risk aversion and risk-taking behaviour depend on wealth outcomes compared to aspiration levels of wealth. Since housing is a major component of wealth (Campbell & Cocco, 2007), SWB housing factors are expected to affect negatively the SWB setpoint when a house bubble bursts as life circumstances changes the aspiration levels on wealth, at least in the short-run. The remaining of the chapter will there­ fore look at the way group behaviour affects life circumstances; how it changes human interactions and how it impacts on resource allocation starting here at the household level, the first point of socialization. 1.3  Group Behaviour in Human Interactions The cognitive biases mentioned so far represent a psychological phenomenon which sustains itself over time with significant economic and human costs. As consumers, investors, migrants, professionals, daughters and fathers, inherited and unconscious roles of behaviours affect all daily decisions and impact the most visible aspects of social life. Social and domestic violence, increasing polarisation and inter-group conflicts are also consequences of these cognitive bias (Wilkinson & Pickett, 2019; Stewart, 2008). Hence, understanding how biases are formed and transmitted is important to link the psychological individual roots of decision-making to the social and economic impact of decision-making. Learning to belong to different group identities is part of the socialisation process and with the household being the first point of socialisation, the following section looks at the way social identities and group membership influences one’s access to resources at the household level. ­ 3 ­ ­ ­ 1.5 Both objective and subjective determinants of wellbeing should be included in the framing of human interactions, and the entitlement framework is useful in that respect. The entitlement framework based on Sen (1981, 1987) proposes to incorpo­ rate the perceived legitimacy of access to resources between social groups, such as gender, and the objectivity of “capabilities” in assessing individual access to resources. At the household level, Sen’s discussion around cooperative conflicts (1987) makes a strong case to move away from traditional household bargaining models which do not adequately account for gender discrepancies in objective and 3 See, among others, Agarwal (1997), Basu (2006), Deere et al. One of his propositions is to expand the informational basis of the household model with “capabilities” and “functionings” to assess objective wellbeing, while keeping a subjective element in wellbeing assessment with per­ ceived interest of the different parties to account “for the causal influence of percep­ tions on ideas of propriety and legitimacy of different institutional arrangements and through that on the respective well-beings of men and women” (Sen, 1987: 5). Bargaining models of resource allocation have moved a long way since Becker’s view (1965) but the essentialist assumption of men versus women with socially ascribed gender characteristics persists. The literature in feminist economics has long shown the importance of moving away from essentialist interpretations of gender differences since it tends to rein­ force gender stereotypes rather than questioning them (Folbre, 2001; Nelson, 2014; Sent & van Staveren, 2019). In experimental behaviour research, most empirical findings tend to promote an essentialist view of gender differences whereby there is either an explicit ascribed dichotomy between genders (e.g. “women are found to be …” ) or an implicit dichotomy “through assuming that men and women make free choices based on their respective innate characteristics” (Sent & van Staveren, 2019: 3). Gender is intrinsically relational and such embedment in the organic nature of the social setting makes it difficult to quantify the economic value of the so-called “feminine” or “masculine” traits without apriorist assumptions based on gender stereotyping, especially as such traits tend to differ across cultural settings (Nelson, 2014; Folbre, 2001). The relational aspect of gender is central to the under­ standing of household relationships as the social construct of “gender” is about being different, not better, being shaped by social relations, over time and space rather than being static (Charles, 2021). ­ 1.6 1987 1987 1.3  Group Behaviour in Human Interactions

This calls for a more fluid definition of “gender” as brought forward by femi­ nist economics in the sense that the perception of gender itself may vary across time and space. Context matters in the way identity is shaped in relation to others, and gender in particular. Such relationality calls for different tacit rules of resource allo­ cation which do not ascribe resources to perceived gender or identity attributes. In turn, different rules of resource allocation, which would be “identity-free” could improve the resilience and flexibility of resource allocation, especially in a context of increasing resource scarcity. It remains to be seen what would serve as a basis for different rules of resources allocation, if any, as will be explored later in the book. Second, both objective and subjective elements of wellbeing are central to the bargaining process (Sen, 1987). In the breakdown position of cooperative conflict when household members fail to cooperate, the resulting position of each member is dependent on both an objective measure of wellbeing—assessed through capa­ bilities; and a subjective measure reflecting the perceived legitimacy of access to resources between the parties (Sen, 1987). The subjective measure will however be bearing the cognitive biases, including group identity, that serve as a basis for decision-­making at the level of remembered utility. Accounting for both objective and subjective wellbeing nonetheless departs from utilitarianism and the use-value of household interactions by incorporating perceptions of legitimacy between mem­ bers in wellbeing assessment and highlighting its role in shaping capabilities in a context of resource scarcity in particular. Social norms in effect convey the rules of legitimacy in access to resources between identity groups where group membership is sustained according to certain ideal criteria of behaviour that sustain group membership. Hence, an individual has multiple identities shaped by social interactions, which entitles him or her to a socially acceptable level of resources (Tienda & Lii, 1987; Massey, 2007; Schippers, 2007). Social identities are endogenous to an individual agency and personal 1  Groupthink in Individual Decision-Making

15 identity as it tends to evolve dynamically over time (Davis, 2011). As such, there is a deterministic element of social life that shapes the way individuals access resources, a perceived legitimacy in social exchange, which depends on the position of the individual’s salient identity on the spectrum of social stratification (Akerlof & Kranton, 2010; Davis, 2011; Darity, 2005; Grusky, 2019). With social norms, individuals consider to be entitled to resources according to their social identities, which provide an incentive to sustain the norm that resources should be ascribed to some rather than others. In times of increasing scarcity, the process of resource allocation follows these rules of allocation more than ever. “Entitlement is essentially a legal concept, dealing with rules that govern who can have the use of what.” (Sen, 1987: 30) Sen has long worked on “entitlements” and failures of access to resources, the theoretical foundations of which served as a basis for the Capability Approach (Sen, 1999). In particular, he argues that the Bengal famine of 1943 was due to entitlement failures to food supply rather than to a short­ age of food supply per se (Sen, 1981). In Sen’s writings the concept of entitlement relates to rules of legitimacy between sets of ownerships whereby “an entitlement relation applied to ownership connects one set of ownerships to another through certain rule of legitimacy. It is a recursive relation and the process of connecting can be repeated.” (Sen, 1981: 1). Since his framework applies to market interactions, the rule of legitimacy depends on trade-based entitlement, production-based entitle­ ment, own-labour entitlement, and inheritance and transfer entitlement. Hence, given that Sen’s approach focuses on market interactions only, the causal link between commodity and utility depends on the individual capability to transform a commodity into utility (Sen, 1999). Thus, the causal link between “commodity” and “utility” is (Clark, 2006): (1) Commodity ➔ Capability (to function) ➔ Function(ing) ➔ Utility, instead of the Utilitarian approach: Commodity ➔ Utility. ­ ­ 1.5 ­ (2) Identity ➔ Commodity ➔ Capability (to function) ➔ Function(ing) ➔ Remembered Utility ➔ Identity; which is one identity-based entitlement relation in market exchange, as a subset of social interactions (3); (3) Identity ➔ Capability (to function) ➔ Function(ing) ➔ Remembered Utility ➔ Identity; 1.6 1.3  Group Behaviour in Human Interactions

16 ­ ­ 1.6 1986 1998 3 1.4  Time, Space and Identity We have seen so far that time matters in the way cognitive biases affect our percep­ tion of life experiences (at time t), but that cognitive biases do not necessarily affect the experience of life itself (at time t-1) which itself is more affected by changes in life circumstances. Yet, we have seen that decision-making at the individual level is based on that perception rather than on life experience itself. This means that, if one looks at the aggregate level of a country for example, hundreds of individual and collective biases will aggregate at the macro-level in a non-systemic fashion, whereby the aggregation of choices by individuals with multiple identities is unpre­ dictable, unless dominant patterns of group behaviour can be identified and acted upon. This is where the concept of “noise” becomes important to understand the aggregation process. Kahneman et al. (2021) in effect make the distinction between the role of cognitive bias and the role of “noise” in decision-making. While cogni­ tive bias and judgements can be accounted for at the aggregate level, and shows in standard deviations, a strong identity element in individual decision-making do influence decisional outcomes in a non-random fashion. At the aggregate level, indi­ vidual decisions can have a strong variance in outcomes which can be referred to as “noise”. Kahneman et al. (2021) take the example of judges in the US court system who, with a similar set of cases, end up with highly dissimilar judgmental out­ comes—with life circumstances such as the time of the day, the mood in the moment, or depending on how sunny the day is, seem to influence the variance in outcomes and hence increasing the noise in the samples collected. On the other hand, when cognitive biases are more dominant than noise on the decision outcome, the 1  Groupthink in Individual Decision-Making

17 decision-­maker seems to recall on the perceived boundaries of group membership as criteria of decision-making, i.e. identities and perceived sense of belonging of individuals are called upon as decision criteria. At the macro-level, we will see in the next chapter how individual biases aggregate in the process of financial accumu­ lation and economic exchanges. The second element strongly impacting on decision-making is space: the indi­ vidual context in which decision-making is made, at the point of remembered util­ ity, i.e. the context in which decision-making takes place influences its outcome. In effect, an exactly similar decision-making process taking place in two different places can lead to two different outcomes. The context in which decisions are made are also shaped by these cognitive biases in the sense that the salient identity of an individual in a particular context will override other identities in a sort of survival strategy. This is why it is important to understand the construction of identity in one space by mapping out the historical dynamics of power which make some identities more dominant than other in human interactions. The work of Suk-Young Chwe (2013) is insightful in that respect as it shows how people who tended to be under­ mined in social interactions, due to slavery for example or in the patriarchal context of the characters in Jane Austen’s novels, tend to develop higher strategic abilities. Slaves and female characters in respective contexts are able to think a few steps ahead of the game in order to be able to survive according to the rules of the game of social legitimacy dictated by the dominant group. Being able to map out the rules of legitimacy that are context-specific is key to understand the rules of human inter­ actions and financial accumulation, as we will now see in Chap. 2. Ultimately, identity is a social construct at the intersection of time—how indi­ vidual’s sense of belonging to groups influence one’s decision and behaviour; and space—how the aggregation od individual biases are context-specific and affect human interactions in one space to the extent that it biases the perception of life experience. Elaborating on Sen’s work on entitlement, we have seen that widen­ ing the spectrum from market to social interactions, with market exchange being a subset of social exchange, the rule of legitimacy over access to resources refer to identity-­based entitlement in exchange. So the main questions the remaining of the book is exploring are: how does groupthink impact on human interactions over time, over space and across identities? How would an economic system look like if all decisions were based on experienced utility, i.e. free from cognitive biases? Would it be a world geared by the invisible hand of Adam Smith and actual trickle down effects? Or would be a theatre of many more conflicts over resources? References Agarwal, B. Charles, Sustainable Earnings in a Resilient Economic System, SpringerBriefs in Economics, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-67573-7_2 Chapter 2 Group Membership in Capital and Labour Earnings Abstract  This chapter provides evidence of how group biases aggregate in the pro­ cess of financial accumulation and the way they affect economic exchange over time. What can we learn on group behaviour from the demographics of capital and labour earnings historically, regionally, nationally and across borders? At the national level, what can we learn from the interdependence of earning trends between groups on the social entitlement rules to financial flows? Being able to map out the rules of legitimacy that are context-specific is key to understanding the tacit rules of human interactions and financial accumulation. Looking at the most visible (data-wise) part of the market economy, the relationships between the historical trends of labour and capital earnings are investigated by gender, race, nationality and occupation for the US, UK and France. It shows that there a two-tier economic system where earnings go in the hands of a few dominant groups at the top of the income distribution, while leaving labour earners with stagnant real-wages. 2.1  Keeping up with the Joneses … But Which Ones? An important factor that has contributed substantially to the 2008 financial crisis and ‘Great recession’ emerged from the steady but sharp rise in the unequal distri­ bution of income between capital and labour, and within labour among different income groups. For instance, in the US the top 1% of households accounted for only 8.9% of income in 1976, but this share grew to 23.5% of the total income generated before the crisis in the summer of 2007 (Rajan, 2010). It has been suggested that the rise in inequality together with financial liberalisation and innovation have gener­ ated the financial crisis, although the mechanisms have differed between the USA (and in part in the UK) and continental EU (Fitoussi & Saraceno, 2010). To under­ stand these mechanisms and the extent to which they differ between the UK and continental Europe, this chapter goes beyond the current literature on income inequality which is looking at the sectoral and industrial income shifts (Galbraith, 2012), or changes in income strata (Atkinson et al., 2011; Milanovic, 2016; Piketty, 2014) to adopt an identity-based approach to income inequality, as I have done in

22 the past (Arestis et al., 2013, 2014; Charles, 2011, 2012; Charles et al., 2011), and to financial accumulation in particular. Financial accumulation here is understood as individual earnings from capital (e.g. capital income such as interest or divi­ dends, inheritance, capital gains, and insurance compensation) and labour (e.g. wages and labour income), which is how I refer here to capital and labour earnings. The elements of groupthink in decision-making described in the previous chap­ ter should show in the patterns of financial accumulation over time. In effect, the “Keeping up with the Joneses” effect has been a triggering factor in enhancing the momentum towards the Great recession, whether it is at the top of managerial and financial occupations with excessive earnings to keep up with the social status of such occupations, or at the bottom of the social ladder where subprime mortgages entertained the dream of feasible access to homeownership for low-income earners. Low-income earners saw homeownership as a possibility because their peers in the group of low-income earners were having access to homeownership. “Keeping up with the Joneses” is a groupthink effect but the issue raised in the previous chapter around the multiple layers of group membership one can identify to leads to the subsequent question: which Joneses? In other words, how do the layers of group membership come out in the dynamics of labour and capital earnings? This chapter therefore seeks to map out financial flows between social groups in the past in order to show the social entitlement rules to financial flows in the past: what can we learn on group behaviour from the demographics of capital and labour earnings historically, regionally, and nationally? At the national level, what can we learn from the interdependence of earning trends between groups on the social enti­ tlement rules to financial flows? The subsequent question for Chap. 3 will then be: how do past social entitlement rules to financial flows feed into the dynamics of future financial flows? 2.2  Group Behaviour in Financial Accumulation 2.2.1  Financial Accumulation: Individual or Group Phenomenon?1 As seen in the previous chapter, the literature distinguishes between group and indi­ vidual behaviour (Bornstein et al., 2004; Charness & Sutter, 2012; Muehlheusser et al., 2015), whereby norms of behaviour by a social group tend to have an impact on individual decision-making. Similarly, in stratification economics, various authors show how race and ethnic group disparities in market outcomes can be sus­ tained and exacerbated over time (Darity & Williams, 1985; Massey, 2007; Grusky & Weisshaar, 2014; Tienda & Lii, 1987). In effect, the relative economic value socially assigned to groups of individuals is mostly historically determined and 1 This section draws from Charles and Sguotti (2021). 2  Group Membership in Capital and Labour Earnings

23 culturally embedded. Social norms convey the rules of legitimacy for the access to resources between social groups, where group membership is sustained according to certain ideal criteria of behaviour that sustain group membership. An individual belongs to multiple identities that are shaped by social interactions, and each iden­ tity socially entitles him or her to a socially acceptable level of resources (Davis, 2011; Akerlof & Kranton, 2010). Social identities are endogenous to an individual’s personal identity since they tend to evolve dynamically over time and thus, ques­ tions the use of methodological individualism to capture the dynamics of inequality between social groups (Davis, 2011). In effect, there is a deterministic element of social life that shapes the way individuals access resources—a perceived legitimacy in social exchanges, which depends on the position of the individual’s identities on the spectrum of context-based social stratification (Davis, 2011; Akerlof & Kranton, 2010; Darity, 2005). When economic exchange takes place, social norms serve as rules for reproduc­ ing the advantages of certain social groups at the expense of others. For instance, in the context of the United States, Arestis et al. (2014) have shown how occupational, race, and gender characteristics are reinforced by the exacerbation of earning dif­ ferentials between demo-graphic groups during the financialization period of 1980–2010. Another example at the intersection of context and educational elites is the evidence from England and Wales that shows that a large number of employers offering the top-paid jobs in the country target an average of only 19 universities (out of 130) in the United Kingdom for those jobs (Dorling, 2013). These examples go beyond the issue of statistical discrimination since group productivity is not responsible for income inequality across all occupations (Tomaskovic-Devey & Skaggs, 1999). Rather, the problem lies in the combined effect of identities on inequality since the sum of identities can lead to worse discriminating outcomes than when considering identities separately, as argued by the intersectionality litera­ ture (hooks, 2015; Crenshaw, 1989; McCall, 2005). Compared with implicit dis­ crimination (Bertrand et al., 2005) or with Becker’s taste discrimination, the concept of intersectionality departs from methodological individualism by questioning the boundaries that can be drawn between groups and by defining individuals by a unique combination of diverse groups. As such, it allows us to assess the multiple layers of discrimination over time, one layer of which is gender. Methodologically, trying to grasp the multiple layers of group belonging over time is challenging. First, using traditional regression methods on individual income or earnings as dependent variable with a range of independent individual variables around education, skills or experience means that the dynamic element will be left in the residuals of the regression. It means that the power dynamics at play over time between groups in access to education, skills or experience will not be visible in the explanatory power of the regression. Instead, as will be presented below with the experience of the US, the UK and France, the method used for each case is based on analysing the trends of group rather than individual earnings. Analysing trends could be done via vector autoregressions (VAR) or cointegration analysis, depend­ ing on the nature of the trends. For example, Arestis et al. (2014) conducted cointe­ gration analysis on labour earnings between demographic groups in the US since 2.2  Group Behaviour in Financial Accumulation

24 1980. Such method allows to reveal the long-term relationship(s) in earnings between demographic groups but it is constrained by the number of data points available for significant results, and such demographic time-series are rarely avail­ able across countries and over long time-series. Second, the power dynamics in the multiple layers of group membership evolves over time in a way that makes it difficult to track empirically. For example, in the Current Population Survey (King et al., 2010), if you track down financial occupa­ tions back in time, the currently known “financial” occupations were “technician” occupations in the late 1970s. However, over time, the social status of financial occupations has risen to such an extent over time that they now belong to the top “managerial and financial” occupations. Similarly, another statistical issue is the lack of visibility of group membership which are simply non-existent. For example, collecting race-based data is still taboo in France due to the traumas of WWII. In effect, a 1978 law bans the collection and storage of race-based data which means that no race or ethnic data exists in one of the most multi-cultural societies of the West. A consequence is that problems of discrimination are not statistically visible, which present issues of transparency and accountability in discriminatory practices against racial and ethnic groups. 2.2.2  Group Example: Gender in Financial Accumulation2 Over the past forty years, the process of financialization in Western economies has had significant distributional effects on the global income distribution, often rein­ forcing existing gender inequalities. Fukuda-Parr et  al. (2013) demonstrate how such dynamics in income distribution at the macroeconomic level have been rein­ forced over the past 40 years. Financial institutions and intermediaries have devel­ oped financial instruments that enable the expansion of lending in the housing sector and in parts of the household economy that were previously deemed too risky to lend to: “the so-called subprime loans were “predatory” (a term that refers to loans made under unfair, deceptive, or fraudulent conditions in the loan origination pro­ cess), targeted to people of color and single female heads of households” (2013: 9). Here, for the US experience, the macroeconomic processes of financial liberaliza­ tion have exacerbated the existing social stratification by race, ethnicity and gender. From the relational lens on gender, financial crises are intrinsically related to the meaning of “gender” and the consequent crisis of “masculinity” emerging globally as a consequence of financial crises. In effect, Fukuda-Parr et al. (2013) argue that “[t]here is evidence from recent financial crises that, due to norms of masculinity, there is a greater tendency for unemployed men to suffer from shame and inade­ quacy upon loss of their breadwinning status, so much so that in some countries men’s suicide rates rise in periods of crisis” (2013: 23). In the Global North, 2 This section draws from Charles (2021). 2  Group Membership in Capital and Labour Earnings

25 financial liberalization meant that investments in physical assets and factories were becoming less attractive than speculative investments in financial markets, i.e. the rate of return on financial capital was more rewarding than investment in tradition­ ally more “masculine” construction and manufacturing sectors. At the global level, such gender norms are also visible in the way financial liberalization, which includes trade liberalization, leads to an expanded use of cheap female wage labour, drawing female labour away from the unpaid household economy to the paid economy—and export-processing zones in particular. When a financial crisis hits the global econ­ omy, demand for manufactured goods decreases and threatens the employment of women, generally dominant in export-led industries, representing for instance 85% of labour in the garment industry in Bangladesh, and 85% in cut flowers in Uganda (Walby, 2009). Over time, the pre-existing gender norms are affected by a rebalanc­ ing of female bargaining power with previously unemployed women now bringing an income in the household economy, thus challenging the traditional breadwinner model and the ideals of “masculinity” within it. The model proposed by Elson (2010) in the context of the global crisis post-2008 seeks to map out the socio-economic dynamics at play in the way a financial crisis affects the social bond in labour markets and the household. Elson offers three dif­ ferent rounds of effects in the financial, productive, reproductive spheres and these rounds of effects essentially depend on the gender interactions between the different spheres and the timeframe adopted, short-run and long-run effects. For example, during a crisis, when paid employment and social welfare tend to be cut, there is an increasing need for the unpaid care economy to fill in the relational gaps left by such cuts. Hence, this adds further pressure on the reproduction sphere and strains further the relations between household members, thus affecting the quality of interactions and functioning of the household unit. Similarly to the increase in racism towards minority groups in relation to a dominant group during periods of adverse economic conditions (Vargas et al., 2018), a recession exacerbates the gender relationship of “feminine” versus “masculine” ideals. The impact of the financial shortage damages the social fabric by threatening the ideal of masculinities with increased suicide rates, rising domestic violence, family abandonment by household heads in the reproductive sphere together with a deterioration of employment opportunities for men, and cuts in welfare support for working mum in the productive sphere (Floro & Dymski, 2000; Karamessini & Rubery, 2013). Post-1997, the experience of Asia facing cuts in welfare services put further pressure on the household economy with increasing debts, job losses and declining incomes (Floro & Dymski, 2000). While the social bond was severely affected by a crisis, the strength of the Asian social bond sustained in the reproductive sphere also meant that it acted as a social safety net since many households survived thanks to family and community links. Across studies, the gendered impact of financial crises on the labour market tends to depend on the quality of the social bond between the three spheres, i.e. depending on how well women’s work is embedded in social norms and expecta­ tions (Lopez-Andreu & Rubery, 2018). When comparing women’s employment tra­ jectories in the UK and Spain during the Great Recession, Lopez-Andreu and Rubery (2018) show that the type of austerity measures and the degree to which 2.2  Group Behaviour in Financial Accumulation

26 they affect the reproductive sphere will subsequently affect the productive sphere, depending on the gender division of labour by occupation and contract type. This echoes similar findings by Peinado and Serrano (2018) who looked at the evolution of gender gaps in employment, earnings and unemployment before and after 2008 in France, the UK, Spain and Italy. Gender norms are here strong drivers of earning and occupational disparities, and such norms have been reinforced by the Great Recession. The overall pattern here is towards the reduction of gender gaps in employment and unemployment but mainly due to worsening outcomes for men in “masculine” occupations such as construction, and an increase in the precarization of employment, such as part-time employment where female labour participation is high. Context-dependency in gender inequality is also described with, for example, high sensitivity to shocks for Spain compared with France, which point out to dif­ ferent gender relationships within the household and the labour market together with country-specific social policies and labour market regulations. Similar findings are found in Karamessini and Rubery (2013) who, across nine case studies, demon­ strate that while there was a deterioration in men’s employment in the aftermath of the crisis, the austerity policies have more than offset this deterioration with its negative effects on the demand for female labour and for services supporting work­ ing mothers. As a consequence, they argue that austerities measures have reinforced “the same failed mechanisms that caused the crisis in the first place and is stalling or even reversing the long-term growth in social investment in support for care.” Hence, any policy route that would sensibly address the causes and consequences of a financial crisis should place gender equality at its core. In non-Western economies, the gendered impact of financial crises on the labour force is also deeply linked to the quality of the social between the three spheres. For example, in the context of the Asian financial crisis of the late 1990s, the impact on the labour market in the Philippines did not necessarily mean higher levels of unem­ ployment for women than men, but it meant longer hours in formal employment and unpaid care employment (Walby, 2009). This is perhaps one of the key points in understanding the gendered impact of financial crisis compared to other social groups present in the labour market; that the overrepresentation of women in the invisible informal and unpaid economy makes it hard to quantify and trace the extent of the damage on women’s livelihoods and on economic development in long-run. A comprehensive study by Blanton et al. (2019) has however assessed the impact of financial crises (currency crises, banking crises, inflation crises and debt crises) on women’s wellbeing across 68 countries from 1980 to 2010 with different time lags since the end of a crisis. The findings consistently show the struggles women face in participating in the formal economy and in the public sphere, while also experiencing declines in health outcomes and educational achievement, up to seven years after a crisis ends. From a relational lens on gender, economic recovery would precisely place care and gender equality at its heart. In line with Karamessini and Rubery (2013), Bargawi and Cozzi (2017) are in favour of engendering the economic recovery from a financial crisis which go through investment in “feminine” types of sectors such as health, care and education services, rather than traditional investments in “mas­ culine” types of sectors such as constructions and physical infrastructure. 2  Group Membership in Capital and Labour Earnings

27 Gender-­sensitive budgets at the macro-level, and fiscal policies supporting “femi­ nine” types of sectors can improve women’s visibility in the economy, as long as such effort is not undermined by austerity measures which tend to transmit the bur­ den of budget cuts on the informal and household economy. Neo-classical austerity measures as such totally misunderstands the relational aspects of market and nonmarket outcomes, which goes back the essence of its starting assumption on selfinterest where the “self” is atomistic and gender neutral. Hence, a gendered approach that alleviates the negative impact of financial crises on women needs to carefully consider the intertwined effects of the financial, productive and reproductive spheres of the economy (Elson, 2010). In effect, investments in the financial or productive spheres without support in the reproductive sphere might indeed have counterpro­ ductive effects in terms of aggregate welfare, cancelling out the initial support given. Instead of classical duality of gender, one must look at the synergies between genders and across the three spheres for the economy to be resilient in the event of a crisis, but also for preventing financial crises in the first place. For example, in the context of the climate and health crises of the 2020s, the duality of gender vanishes if one applies the perceived feminine attribute of “care” to the traditional “mascu­ line” sectors of construction or finance. In effect, the essential criterion in decisionmaking for the construction sector should be the long-term impact on environmental and human health. As such governments should be making “mission-oriented” investments with private-public partnerships for a Green New Deal (Mazzucato, 2021). Similarly, in the financial sector, reaping the long-term benefits for environ­ mental and human health should be the key criterion for successful green bonds provided by investment banks, rather than allowing speculative bubbles to be freely built up by herd-behaviour and social status-seeking in financial markets, with its devastating effects on the long-run sustainability of the economy. Box 2.1 Methodological Warning: Group-Based Data and Data Availability The empirical analyses in this Chapter make use of individual-level data aggregated at the group level. As such, it allows to focus on the explanatory power of group membership in the dynamics of accumulation of capital and labour earnings. Hence, Augmented Dickey Fuller (ADF) tests are conducted on time-series group earnings to be able find potential differences between groups on the nature of their earning variables (Tables 2.1 and 2.2), and Vector Auto-Regressions (VARs) of paired earnings between two demographic groups at a time are also performed to analyse the relationships between group earnings (Tables 2.3 and 2.4). The lack of availability of long-run time-­ series on demographic earnings by identity group across countries means that not enough data points were available to run a cointegration analysis, as done previously in Arestis et al. (2014). This calls for a more systematic collection of socio-demographic characteristics for income and wealth data over time, at the household, national and international level. 2.2  Group Behaviour in Financial Accumulation

28 2.3  Labour Earnings by Race, Ethnicity, Gender and Occupation 2.3.1  The US Experience (1968–2011) Using the Current Population Survey (CPS) data (King et al., 2010), this first case study looks at the long-run behaviour of earnings by gender and racial groups across occupations in the US labour force between 1968 and 2011. In accordance with the literature on the US stratification using CPS data (Arestis et al., 2014), the gender and racial identity group included are white men (wm), black men (bm), Hispanic men (hm), white women (wf), black women (bf), and Hispanic women (hf). We use the current annual weekly earnings of the above mentioned identity groups for 27 consistent occupational groups over the period 1968–2011, as displayed in Table 2.1, respectively. Earnings are the annual average of usual weekly earnings of employed full-time wage and salary workers by group. Using Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) tests, the methodology consists of testing whether the earnings of each identity group in each occupation are non-­stationary, trend-stationary or stationary over the analysed period. By doing so, we are able to categorise the pattern followed by the earnings of each group across occupations according to the nature of the long-run trend. We use nominal instead of real earn­ ings to account for money illusion including price stickiness, and lack of inflationindexation on labour contracts and laws. We use means rather than median earnings in order to account for the information provided by outliers. In other words, we are interested in exploring the raw information provided by groups’ earnings along the income stratification spectrum. If the earnings variable of an identity group is non-stationary, it means that there is a persistent cumulation of past effects (shocks) (Hendry & Juselius, 2001) leading to sustained changes in earnings. If the earnings variable of an identity group is stationary, it means that their earnings remain constant over the period. Stationary earnings are not benefiting from the increase in occupa­ tional earnings over the period and they are assumed to be compensating for a move­ ment of income towards non-stationary earnings. Hence, non-­stationary (stochastic trend) earnings are “elitist” in comparison to trend-stationary (deterministic-trend) or stationary earnings in the sense that a percentile of income distribution experi­ ences shocks that cumulate in the long-run while other percentiles do not. In effect, trend-stationary “non-elitist” earnings represent a percentile of income distribution whose long-run trend grow at an arithmetic rate, while stationary “non-elitist” earn­ ings represent a percentile of income distribution whose long-run trend is constant. Looking at Table 2.1, apart from health and personal services with 89 and 78% female labour force, it shows that white men experience non-stationary earnings across all occupations. In comparison, black and Hispanic men experience trend-­ stationary and/or stationary earnings in many occupations, in professional occupa­ tions in particular. Black men experience stationary and trend-stationary earnings in a wider variety of occupations than Hispanic men. 35 2.4  Group “Legitimacy” in Financial Flows3 Starting from Charles and Vujic (2018), we assumed a society with two demo­ graphic groups, i and j, both belonging to the same occupational group k. Therefore, individuals are composed of groups i and k or of group identities j and k. A socially dominant group is represented by j and receives a premium for group membership, while the non-dominant group is represented by i, whose earnings are discriminated against due to group membership. Hence, we assumed a ranking of groups of j > i, dependent upon the context specificity in which this ranking has been socially and historically determined. 3 This section draws from Charles and Sguotti (2021). Box 2.2 Methodological Warning: Causality Vs. Correlation In mainstream economics textbooks, we learn that individual income is a function of a variety of human capital factors, such as marginal productivity, educational background, skills, and so on. Such methodological individual­ ism means that the discriminatory elements of socialization attached to gen­ der, race, class, ethnicity and other social identities are embedded across those individual characteristics and are, as such, not fully accounted for to explain the variance in individuals’ income. As a result, when seeking causal links to explain the variance in income using first-differences, the historical elements of discrimination accumulated over time may end up in the residual of a tra­ ditional regression. However, such discriminatory elements describing the power relationships between social groups in a particular context become central to the way income is distributed and hence the way wealth is accumu­ lated over time. “Correlation is not causality” we have been taught, and that’s right. However, correlation tells us a story of relationality between variables whose inherent nature lie in the long-term relationship that have generated engrained long-term links difficult to depart from—similarly to the cognitive biases deeply engrained in remembered utility. We have been taught to “de-­ naturalize” time series data by de-trending, differentiating and searching for immutable causal links. However, when context shapes economic outcomes, the causals links A ➔ B and B ➔ C in one context might become B ➔ A and C ➔ B in another. Hence, the methodology of the time-series analysis in this chapter (1) uses level data to keep the nature of the time series alive, including potential structural breaks, and then applies (2) Augmented Dickey Fuller (ADF) tests on group earnings to analyse the nature of the long-run trends, and (3) Vector Autoregression (VAR) to analyse the nature of the relationships between group earnings. As such, we can highlight the context and nature of the relations present in the time series analysed. 2.4  Group “Legitimacy” in Financial Flows

Some social groups earn more at the expense of others, which is based on social relationships of power more than on individual productivity. There is, therefore, the evidence here of the interdependency of earnings between social groups, whether it is in the United Kingdom, France, or Italy, with varying degrees of interdependency across groups and countries. Such discrepancies are not based on individual productivity but on group biases, whereby some groups are deemed socially and, therefore, economically more valuable than others. Over time, such discrepancies are economically unsustainable, feeding into herd behaviour that exac­ erbates group status and eventually creating production, consumption, and finan­ cially speculative bubbles that sustain the social status of the dominant group, making the entire economic system unsustainable. Another methodological perspective on financial accumulation is therefore needed for a sustainable economic system. When looking at its impact on resource allocation, group behaviour has fed into the Great Acceleration with its associated patterns of consumption of fossil fuel, natural and financial resources, and it is still prevalent today as a tacit rule for resource allocation. The pattern of earnings accumulation in Western economies is still dependent upon colonial and patriarchal dominance of certain dominant groups at the expense of dominated groups. The overall finding from both Tables is that there is no significant relationships between the past and present earnings of minority groups, while most significant relationships exist for the dominant groups, White and Male in the UK sample, and the French nationality group in the France sample. For example, in Table 2.5, it doesn’t make “economic” sense to have the past earnings of non-French groups being positively associated with the present earnings of the French nationality group. Similarly, looking at capital earnings across occupations, it doesn’t make economic sense for male capital earnings at time t to be positively associated with female capital earnings at time t-1, and it provides yet more evidence for a system of financial accumulation based on group rather than individual behaviour. 2.5  Towards Sustainable Earnings? While the global patterns of wealth accumulation have been well-documented by Piketty (2014, 2019), and that income inequality tends to be broken down by income strata (Milanovic, 2016), or sectoral level (Galbraith, 2012), dividing earnings between labour and capital is a methodological choice which allows to investigate the dynamics of income accumulation in both the labour and capital shares of national income. Segregating further by demographic group is a theoretical choice which, depending on data availability by country, highlights the patterns of income accumulation affected by group membership. Group memberships are in effect set­ ting the tacit rules of income distribution at the margin and hence over time. In such a dynamic system of social relationships, analysing financial flows takes us back to the classical literature on the nature of money with trust being at to the heart of the meaning of money from Aristotle to Keynes (Eich, 2022). In a dynamic system of financial flows based of social relationships, trust is shaped by those tacit rules. Over the past forty years, the pattern of financial accumulation based of those tacit rules have led to a mistrust and misfunctioning of the economic system to self-­ regulate income accumulation. The financialisation process fed by a process of “financing finance” (Mazzucato, 2021) is now leading to a two-tier system going in the hands of a few dominant groups at the top of the income distribution, while leav­ ing labour earners with stagnant real-wages at the bottom. This Chapter also shows that dominated groups have experienced a colonisation of their labour earnings based of vicious marginal increases for some groups at the expense of other groups. Meanwhile, mapping the social identity elements of those few would lead to a biased sample of the global human population, but such demographic data is not available. So, are the current patterns of group accumulation sustainable? Well, if sustain­ ability is understood as a self-sustaining process of earning accumulation, then the current tacit rules on group norms are certainly self-sustainable and here to stay. However, if sustainability is understood as the extent to which current earnings feed into a resilient economic system able to feed the financial needs of sustaining life on Earth, then no. 2.5  Towards Sustainable Earnings?

Charles, Sustainable Earnings in a Resilient Economic System, SpringerBriefs in Economics, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-67573-7_3 Chapter 3 Freeing the Collective Mind: Making Decisions With or Without Group Biases Abstract  This chapter shows that group membership and its associated cognitive bias within the self makes the assumption of “individual” decision-making prob­ lematic in that it creates a cognitive illusion of the “self” versus “others”, when the self is in essence dynamic and relational. The consequence of such illusion is a mir­ ror effect in resource allocation based on group bias. It makes the whole system of resource allocation entirely reliant on the arbitrary nature of human perception, which differ across individuals. Aggregating group biases at the macro-level then leads to herd behaviour which can have a positive or negative impact on resource allocation, consumption and conservation. Group dynamics can however work towards resource allocation and conservation if decisions are made without group biases at the micro-level, or if group biases are regulated at the macro level.  1 If we account for groupthink in individual-decision-making seriously, the bound­ aries around the self in the “self-interest” assumption become blurred. This is not to argue around altruistic vs. self-interested motives in decision-making. Rather, group membership and its associated cognitive bias within the self makes the fun­ damental assumption of “individual” decision-making problematic. In effect, at an ontological level, neo-classical economics is underpinned by an implicit assump­ tion of the “essentialist self”, where the self-interest of the consumer or the pro­ ducer, as utility-­maximiser and profit-maximiser respectively, is treated as the ‘natural’ and ‘universal’ self, and those not closely resembling one or the other are treated as ‘other’. Separating the self and other results in the other being devalued and marginalised relative to the self. This is an argument developed further in Bondy and Charles (2020) around stakeholder theory and on which this section is based. 1 This section draws from Bondy and Charles (2020).

52 Looking at the essentialist self on the basis of gender in traditional Western thinking, the concept of man is associated with autonomy, independence, and ratio­ nality, whereas the concept of woman is associated with relationships, connected­ ness and subjectivity (Nelson, 1997, 2014). These characteristics often hold as ‘natural facts’ (Flax, 1987), where men embody such things as freedom and ratio­ nality as an extension of being a man, whereas women embody such things as con­ nectedness and interdependence as an extension of being a woman (Gilligan, 1982). Based on this view, we can understand the essence of ‘man’ or ‘woman’ through these ‘natural facts’. They tell us what it means to be man or woman beyond differ­ ences in biology (Budgeon, 2014). Given that in contemporary Western societies we tend to value such characteristics as rationality and independence, over connected­ ness and interdependence, it allows us to legitimately prefer those embodying highly valued characteristics—men—and marginalize those with poorly valued characteristics—women (Warren, 1990). Thus the deconstruction of this essentialist view is fundamental to understanding the problematic nature of gender relations where ‘man’ is perceived as the ‘universal, natural self’ and ‘woman’ is devalued as ‘other’ (Flax, 1987). The first problem with the essentialist self is that it does not relate to experienced utility (Fig. 1.2) as it does not reflect the lived experience of most people. With cat­ egorizations like those mentioned above, the self cannot move between sides of the dichotomy (e.g. man OR woman) without risking marginalization (Butler, 2004). For instance, transsexual and transgender people do not fit neatly into one or the other side of the dichotomy during some, or all, of their lives (Doan, 2010). It is also quite clear that not all women can be described as connected, interdependent and/or subjective, nor all men rational, independent and/or autonomous. Thus, these traits are neither ‘natural’ (Flax, 1987), nor demonstrative of the essence of man or woman, but reflect the social experience of the gender dichotomy. In fact, very few male individuals, for example, fit into a category that presumed ‘man’ to refer to white, wealthy, heterosexual and with a professional qualification. In fact, this mar­ ginalizes most of ‘men’ that have ever been, or are now currently alive. In this way, the essentialist view of the self marginalizes most people, leaving only an elite that is socially perceived as the ‘universal’ self and hence dominant within social relations. The second key concern with the essentialist self is that it is static, setting in stone cognitive biases at the level of remembered utility and hence disconnecting the self from the individual context (see Fig. 1.6). In the gender example, once we know the essence of ‘man’ or ‘woman’, these traits are held as relevant regardless of time or context. Work on masculinity and femininity in the socialist feminist tradition has fundamentally challenged this notion (Connell, 1995). Not only has it sought to separate ‘man’ or ‘woman’ from the traits associated with particular gen­ ders, but to demonstrate that these traits belong to all genders without losing the historical context in which the traits developed (Derry, 1996). These traits, or mas­ culine and feminine ideals, change over time in relation to each other, and therefore require an analysis of their social practice in relation to other practices and social change, over time (Schippers, 2007). Men as ‘risk-takers’ is a recent phenomenon 3  Freeing the Collective Mind: Making Decisions With or Without Group Biases

53 that only works in relation to women as ‘prudential’. Thus, the simple social dichot­ omy, ‘man’ OR ‘woman’, is in fact the production of changing social relations and their historical context, rather than any objective identification of core biological characteristics specific to a sex. Feminist theory thus proposes an alternative to the essentialist self, called the relational self.  2 The concept of a relational self builds upon the idea that each self is composed of multiple, intersecting selves, that while different and sometimes in conflict, do not privilege one over another, and are constantly shaped and challenged through social relations and personal introspection within relevant contexts. This section discusses these three overlapping ideas in further detail. 3.2.1  Intersectionality and Multiple Identities First, intersectionality depicts the self at the intersection of several identities, and not a fixed essence based on a particular biological form (Crenshaw, 1989). Rather, the self is composed of multiple, heterogeneous ‘others’ which combine to create a self whose meaning is in relation to the other, framed within contextual hierarchies. So instead of the ‘man’ OR ‘woman’ dichotomy, intersectionality suggests that there are multiple identities such as academic, women, mother, eco-warrior, friend, partner, social activist etc. that interweave into a whole, dynamic self that shifts and is shaped in relation to other relational selves (McCall, 2005). This is not to say that the whole self is harmonious. Rather, each identity contributes in unique ways to the heterogeneity of the self and these, sometimes, conflicting selves reflect the indi­ vidual’s lived experience. Intersectionality thus dismantles the assumption that all women or men are the same (Nash, 2008), but rather the self is composed of a unique combination of multiple identities interrelating through social structures and that characterize how an individual experiences her/his life. 3.2.2  Different, Not Better Second, a relational self rejects the assumption that dichotomies presume opposites, and that opposites allow us to give a higher value to one side or the other (Butler, 2004). A relational self, with multiple intersecting identities does not presume any 2 This section also draws from Bondy and Charles (2020). 3.2  Dynamic and Relational Self

54 one characteristic as more or less valuable, but as different and therefore more or less prevalent in different contexts. Nelson’s (1992) work highlights the dispropor­ tionate value given to opposites on the gender dichotomy in the context of Western thinking, and the social relations that create and maintain it. She first argues that masculine traits are far more often viewed as positive, and feminine traits as nega­ tive. She then invites us to reflect on the positive/negative counterparts of character­ istics so as to neutralize the higher/lower, better/worse types of value associated with the trait. In this way, she demonstrates that gender images are ideals based on people’s imagination, collective and cultural norms, and so is the value proscribed to them. As such, they can be reconstituted as differences, rather than opposites on a dichotomy, which can thus be merged to form a heterogeneous self not ascribed to fixed, perceived attributes that privilege one over the other. The relational self there­ fore recognizes a unique, multi-dimensional, introspective and relational self, where no trait or identity is privileged or marginalized, and that sits at the crossroads of multiple social groups. 3.2.3  Shaped by Changing Social Relations Third, a relational self is a self that is shaped in interaction with other relational selves, and both shapes, and is shaped by, dynamic social structures (e.g. Borgerson, 2007) that change over time and space (e.g. Charles, 2012). In other words, to understand the self, we look at the perceived attributes of others and, through intro­ spection, form our personal identity in relation to the identities of other groups. In the latest wave of transnational feminism, the perception of social identities is context-­based and founded on globalised ideals of femininity and masculinity (e.g. Pearson, 2007), as well as ideals of other social groups such as race, ethnicity, occu­ pation, nationality etc. (e.g. Charles, 2012), that constantly evolve in relation to one another. As such, defining the self is as much about the unique composition of selves that form the whole, as it is about the way each self defines itself relative to other social groups. ­ ­ 1.6 3.1 3.3 3  Freeing the Collective Mind: Making Decisions With or Without Group Biases

Here, the social rules of legitimacy in access to resources rule the process of resource allocation. As such, the proposition is that there is a mirror effect in resource entitlements whereby one’s resource entitlements is based on others’ resource entitlements rather than on his or her actual access to resources. In simple terms, it means that “what you have/ have not” reflects on “what I consider to have/have not” regardless of resource availability. 3.3 3.2 ­ ­ 3  Freeing the Collective Mind: Making Decisions With or Without Group Biases

61 3.4  Freeing the Collective Mind: With or Without Group Biases? With a mirror effect, the self keeps the illusion of making decisions freely when it is actually based on remembered utility where the comfort of group biases lies, among other cognitive biases. It is comfortable in the sense that it reduces the uncer­ tainty linked to life choices when decision-making then relies more on the perceived boundaries of group membership (such as group preferences or characteristics) than on life experience at the point of experienced utility. Consequently, the perception of life at the point of remembered utility is tainted through the lens of group biases, bounced back through the mirror effect. It then leads to herd behaviour in the way group biases per individual aggregate in a cumulative fashion. Herd behaviour then have a positive or negative impact on resource allocation, consumption and conser­ vation. The question now is whether individual freedom of choice is just an illusion in the context of group biases. In effect, let me reframe the question to whether “freedom” of choice with group bias is a valid basis for “individual” decision-­ making, or is it rather an illusion of individual freedom. If so, then alleviating group biases can free the collective mind of the potential negative impact they have on resource allocation, consumption and conservation. To understand how to alleviate group biases in individual and collective decision-­ making, we will now look at potential positive and negative impacts of group behav­ iour. So far, in Chaps. 1 and 2, we have looked at “negative” examples of herd behaviour. Relevant examples have included the demographics of discrimination in financial accumulation in Western economies (Darity, 2005; Arestis et al., 2014; Charles, 2021), but it also extends to inter-group conflicts worldwide (Stewart, 2008), herd-behaviour on global demand with the example of the consumption of textiles leading to water depletion in China (Li et al., 2017). Positive examples of herd-behaviour include numerous social movements that led to positive societal and environmental changes such as the movement leading to the widespread use of bicy­ cles in the Netherlands, the Fridays For Future movement, or the #MeToo and #BlackLivesMatter movements globally. Those examples, both positive and negative, illustrate the fact that the impact herd-behaviour is not predictable. At the micro-level, cognitive mechanisms of group biases affect remembered utility which serves as a basis for decision-making. This means that there is a propensity for the narrative of dominant groups to be imposed on the rest of the world. And, as witnessed by colonisation regimes on the land and sea, dominance is a proxy for ownership (Charles & Blondel, 2023). Hence, at the macro-level, the cumulative effect of group biases leads both to a dis­ tortion of resource allocation towards dominant groups, but also to the deterioration of natural resources that herd-behaviour brings, as witnessed by the Great Acceleration. ­ 3.4  Freeing the Collective Mind: With or Without Group Biases?

Principles (1), (2), (4) and (5) are present in the eight sites with no institutional failures, and they all relate to strong group membership and its associated norms of behaviour to effectively manage the commons locally. The design principles (1), (2), (4) and (5) are behavioural rules engrained at the level of remembered utility for individuals in the sites investigated and they have been so for hundreds of years in some cases. However, while such community-led management systems are powerful in making use of norms and group behaviour, it is not clear how such mechanisms can be scaled-up at a regional, national or global level of resource allocation. In effect, while the strength of group membership in Ostrom’s framework relies on group membership designed around resource conser­ vation, once market exchange takes place, the financial transaction breaks the cog­ nitive link between decision-making and the local context. In market exchange, group membership removes the “self” from their context of decision-making, or experienced utility, and uses the boundaries of group member­ ship instead as a basis for decision-making, or in other words remembered utility. Such cognitive process removes the cognitive link of decision-making from the eco­ logical context and potential ecological impact of market decisions. The ecological context of decision-making however matters, and ecological rationality has long argued that the context in which decision-making takes place influences the out­ come decision and its environmental impact (Gigerenzer & Todd, 1999). This makes community-based initiatives such as the ones studied by Ostrom successful in con­ serving natural resources and embracing local priorities in a way that preserve that cognitive link to the ecological context. Promoting group membership around local resource use can be illustrated by numerous other examples of community-led interventions that have been successful in resource conservation (Krasny et al., 2011). Examples include the community-­ led initiatives triggered by the theoretical framework of Doughnut Economics (Raworth, 2017), but also civil society organisations pushing for sustainable devel­ opment (Asia Civil Society Partnership for Sustainable Development, Arab NGO Network for Development, or the Pacific Islands Association of NGOs), and the numerous coastal community-based initiatives for ocean conservation (Charles & Blondel, 2023). Finally, there is now a widespread recognition that indigenous knowledge is vital for the local implementation of the SDGs (Global Sustainable Development Report, 2023). In the light of such locally-based initiatives, the future promises to be made of islands of excellence in resource conservation, while the allocation of resources in between may or may not remain prone to herd-behaviour, as we will now see. 3.4  Freeing the Collective Mind: With or Without Group Biases?

66 3.4.2  Macro-level: Aggregating and Alleviating Group Biases In Western economies, at the macro-level, we have seen in Chap. 3 that there is now a two-tier system where, at the top of the income distribution, financialisation led to “financing finance” (Mazzucato, 2021) going in the hands of a few dominant groups, while leaving labour earners with stagnant real-wages in the second tier. Domination here is again used as a proxy for ownership, similarly to maritime colonisation regimes (Charles & Blondel, 2023), or at least the illusion of ownership through the lens of group bias leading to the real control of resources. Tackling the negative impact of group biases means that policy interventions should re-allocate resources to alleviate such negative impact while promoting the positive impact of group biases. For pro-environmental behaviour for example, we know that the types of interventions influencing the choice made by individuals, the so-called “downstream” interventions such as information, advertising, education and social approaches, tend to be 2–3% effective. Meanwhile, the so-called “upstream” interventions influencing the context of decision-making such as eco­ nomic policy, nudges, regulations and changes to built environment tend to be up to 100% effective (Nisa et al., 2019; Verplanken & Wood, 2006). This confirms the importance of ecological rationality to account for context in policy-making, but it also begs the question as to why influencing individual choices are not so effective. To be effective in market exchange, downstream interventions need to promote decision-making at the point of experienced utility where the cognitive link to the ecological context of decision may still be alive. We see it in the way that paying for a resource often removes the individual’s responsibility from the impact of its con­ sumption. A concrete example is the illusion that carbon markets create by issuing a license to pollute instead of cutting for carbon emissions in absolute terms. Instead, downstream interventions should first identify the boundaries of group member­ ships involved in market exchange by gathering data on group membership, and then targeting the responsibility of individual behaviour by showing the link between individual and group behaviour on the one hand, and showing the link between the group’s revealed preferences and its environmental impact on the other hand. If not effective in targeting experienced utility, then downstream interventions in market exchange should target remembered utility directly, re-allocating resources systemi­ cally so as to remove the cognitive biases affecting negatively resource allocation, and encouraging cognitive biases affecting resource allocation positively. For exam­ ple, gradual taxes on frequent flyers based on Ostrom’s graduated sanctions princi­ ple, alongside subsidies for low-carbon travellers could be effective in alleviating group biases and in promoting positive change. 3.5  Conclusion Overall, this Chapter has shown that group membership and its associated cognitive bias within the self makes the assumption of “individual” decision-making prob­ lematic in that it creates a cognitive illusion of the “self” versus “others”, when the 3  Freeing the Collective Mind: Making Decisions With or Without Group Biases

67 self is in essence dynamic and relational. The consequence of such illusion is a mir­ ror effect in resource allocation based on group bias. It makes the whole system of resource allocation entirely reliant on the arbitrary nature of human perception, which differ across individuals. Aggregating group biases at the macro-level then leads to herd behaviour which can have a positive or negative impact on resource allocation, consumption and conservation. Group dynamics can however work towards resource allocation and conservation if decisions are made without group biases at the micro-level, or if group biases are regulated at the macro level. The next Chapter proposes the concept of sustainable earnings to show how group biases at the macro level could be alleviated or encouraged for a resilient economic system able to channel finance towards sustainable goals.
